points: Synchronised swimming is performing figures and routines to music, either solo or in a group.
It is judged on execution and artistic impression.
The sport is now officially called artistic swimming.
Swim Ireland governs synchronised swimming in Ireland.
Sculling is continuous figure-of-eight hand movement that supports and moves the body.
Standard scull: the basic sculling movement.
Support scull: used in vertical positions to hold the body up.
Propelling scull: used to move the body through the water.

notes.h: Back layout, front layout and tuck position
points: Back layout: floating on the back, with the body straight and horizontal.
Back layout: the face, chest, thighs and feet are at the surface.
Front layout: face down, with the body straight and horizontal at the surface.
Tuck position: the knees and hips are bent and drawn to the chest, so the body is compact.
Front pike: bent at the hips to 90 degrees, with the legs straight and together and the trunk straight.
The front pike is the starting shape for many figures.
Back pike: bent at the hips to about 90 degrees, with the legs straight and together, facing upwards.
Ballet leg: from the back layout, one leg is raised vertically and kept straight while the other stays at the surface.
Flamingo: a back-based position with one leg extended vertically, as in the ballet leg.
Flamingo: the other leg is drawn up towards the chest, with the shin parallel to the surface.
Vertical positions: the body is vertical and head-down, with the legs extended out of the water.
Fishtail: one leg is vertical, and the other extends forward horizontally at the surface.
Bent-knee vertical: one leg is vertical, and the other is bent with its toe touching the inside of the straight leg's knee.
Surface arch: the lower back is arched, with the legs at the surface.
Dolphin arch: the body is arched as it travels head-first in a circle under the water, as in the dolphin figure.
The split walkover front begins from a front pike or a vertical position.
The legs split and walk over to finish the figure.
Figures move smoothly from one position to another.
Transitions are performed with control, height and stability.
Choreography: a sequence that combines the positions and figures.
Synchronisation: timing with each other and with the music.
Patterns and formations, using the pool space.
Entries and exits.
Expression and artistic impression.
Execution: precision, height, control and synchronisation.
Artistic impression: choreography, musicality and manner of presentation.
Difficulty of the figures.
Breath control and cardio-respiratory endurance.
Flexibility, core strength and leg strength.
Co-ordination and spatial awareness under water.
Concentration and teamwork.
Training takes place in supervised deep water.
Breath-hold training is built up gradually, without hyperventilation.
Nose clips help keep water out of the nose.

keyTerms.definition: Performing figures and routines to music, either solo or in a group.
Continuous figure-of-eight hand movements that support and move the body.
A position floating flat on the front or the back, with the body straight and horizontal.
A compact position with the knees and hips bent and drawn to the chest.
A position bent at the hips to 90 degrees, with straight, together legs and a straight trunk.
A position bent at the hips to about 90 degrees, with straight, together legs, facing upwards.
A back-layout position in which one leg is raised vertically and straight while the other stays at the surface.
A vertical position with one leg vertical and the other extended forward horizontally at the surface.
A back-based position with one leg vertical and the other drawn up, its shin parallel to the surface.
A position with the lower back arched and the legs at the surface.
A position in which the body is arched as it travels head-first in a circle under the water.
A figure in which the legs split and walk over from a front pike or vertical position to finish.

factCards.definition: Standard scull, support scull (in vertical positions) and propelling scull.

questions.prompt: Describe three positions used in synchronised swimming and explain what judges look for in each.
questions.model: Front pike: the body is bent at the hips to 90 degrees, with the legs straight and together and the trunk straight. It is the starting shape for many figures. Judges look for precision in the angle and in the straightness of the legs and trunk, and for height and control as the position is entered and held. Back layout: the body floats on the back, straight and horizontal, with the face, chest, thighs and feet at the surface. Judges look for a straight, horizontal line held with control and stability. Ballet leg: from the back layout, one leg is raised vertically and kept straight while the other stays at the surface. Judges look for a straight, vertical leg held with height and control and, in a duet or trio, synchronisation with the partners.

questions.prompt: Explain the importance of sculling in synchronised swimming.
questions.model: Sculling is a continuous figure-of-eight hand movement that supports and moves the body. The support scull holds the body up in vertical positions, so the performer can keep the upper body out of the water without sinking. The propelling scull moves the body through the water, which lets the performer travel between positions and across the pool. Without sculling, the performer could not hold the vertical shapes or move smoothly through a routine.
